item.title: Ukraine and Russia both report cyberattacks on emergency apps
item.description:
Ukraine and Russia both report cyberattacks on emergency apps
Authorities in Ukraine and Russia have reported cyberattacks on their emergency alert appsByDEREK GATOPOULOS Associated PressNovember 2, 2026, 4:05 AM
Share
KYIV, Ukraine -- Authorities in both Ukraine and Russia say that their emergency alert mobile applications were targeted by cyberattacks late Sunday, with residents in Ukraine receiving messages that there was a high nuclear radiation danger in the capital Kyiv.
In a post late Sunday on Telegram, Ukraine’s air raid alert channel wrote that “unauthorized parties” had interfered with the messaging app’s operation, and that it had been temporarily suspended. It warned users not to click on links contained in “suspicious notifications.”
Authorities in Ukraine said the app, which Ukrainians rely on to seek safety amid daily Russian missile and drone strikes, was restored overnight. The alerts — making false claims of high radiation levels, a chemical threat and public disturbances in Kyiv — were written in English with spelling mistakes and grammatical errors as well as in a mix of Russian and Ukrainian.
One of the false posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore. Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. That claim could not be independently verified.
Ukraine's state-run Center for Countering Disinformation reported the breach and urged users to monitor emergency channels on social media and rely on physical alerts while the cyberattack was being addressed.

item.title: Where things stand on Iran after a tense weekend
item.description:
Where things stand on Iran after a tense weekend
The Middle East is bracing for a potential return to all-out war as concerns grow over possible U.S. and Israeli strikes on IranByCARA ANNA Associated PressNovember 2, 2026, 3:55 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
JERUSALEM -- The Middle East is braced for a possible return to all-out war. There are concerns that the United States, along with Israel, could strike Iran shortly after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the U.S.
Two Iranian officials said their delegation had left Qatar after days of discussions but that messages with the U.S. continued to be exchanged through the mediator. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the talks.
The diplomatic efforts seek to avert new attacks. Tehran has expanded its threats but said it is waiting for the latest U.S. response to a proposal that would fully open the Strait of Hormuz to shipping within two days if Washington meets several conditions.
Here’s where things stand Monday.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday evening told reporters he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a “very good” call on Saturday. He said they discussed Iran but gave no details.
Even before Netanyahu and his bloc of allies lost their majority in parliament in last week’s election, there were growing fears that Netanyahu was pushing for new strikes against Iran in an effort to stay in power in an emergency government during renewed war. Since last Tuesday’s election, the prime minister has publicly commented only on the vote.
There was no word from Netanyahu and his office on the latest call with Trump, who has continued to alternate between public comments about pursuing talks with Iran and threats to strike it hard.
The Islamic Republic has stepped up its public messaging during the uncertainty, saying it is ready for both diplomacy and renewed fighting.

item.title: A brief ceasefire opens a perilous escape window from Kherson’s riverside kill zone
item.description:
A brief ceasefire opens a perilous escape window from Kherson’s riverside kill zone
Nataliia Diadiuk uses a white towel to signal Russian drones that she is a civilian in Ukraine’s Kherson regionByHANNA ARHIROVA Associated Press and VOLODYMYR YURCHUK Associated PressNovember 2, 2026, 12:09 AM
KOZATSKE, Ukraine -- A white towel on her gate and a white rag in her hand were Ukrainian Nataliia Diadiuk’s only ways to tell Russian drone operators she is a civilian. When a brief ceasefire kicked in on Oct. 27, she had a moment of respite.
The 53-year-old is one of a handful of residents left in Kozatske, a riverside village located in the kill zone of Ukraine’s Kherson region less than 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from a Russian-controlled area.
“I really want silence,” Diadiuk said, fighting back tears as she stood on an empty street lined with abandoned houses. “And I want to see the people who left, all of them. People left for both sides."
Diadiuk’s life has been reduced to basic survival: rainwater to drink, firewood gathered around town for heat, a radio she tries to tune in to for news, and the remnants of humanitarian aid that had not reached her in two years until the brief ceasefire that ended Sunday night just days after it began. Going out means dodging every kind of weapon, including mines scattered everywhere. The neighbors she mentions are more often the dead than the few still living nearby.
A team from The Associated Press gained rare access to a so-called red zone to see firsthand what life in the kill zone looks like, a visit made possible only because of a brief, localized ceasefire tied to the humanitarian aid mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

item.title: Dozens of Commonwealth leaders descend on Antigua during global political turbulence
item.description:
Dozens of Commonwealth leaders descend on Antigua during global political turbulence
Leaders representing nearly a third of the world’s population are meeting on the tiny Caribbean island of Antigua this week to strengthen ties during a time of global political upheavalByDÁNICA COTO Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 11:00 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Leaders representing nearly a third of the world’s population are meeting on the tiny Caribbean island of Antigua this week to strengthen ties during a time of global political upheaval.
New deals and pledges are expected to emerge from the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, which is held every two years. More than 50 leaders of Commonwealth nations, many of which once formed part of the British Empire, are scheduled to attend, along with officials from Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Brazil and the United Arab Emirates.
“To deal with what to expect in Antigua, I think we need … to look at the world in which we find ourselves today,” Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey told The Associated Press ahead of the meeting. “We’re looking at issues like conflict, economic shocks, rising costs, climate change, trade, weaponization of tariffs; and all of this hitting directly the pockets of our people.”
Botchwey said Commonwealth leaders representing 2.7 billion people will look at how to attract investment and reduce barriers to intra-Commonwealth trade.
“For us, this is extremely important,” she said. “All the countries woke up one day and were slapped with tariffs. If we are trading more among ourselves, whatever happens outside the Commonwealth will not affect countries too much.”
U.S. President Donald Trump has imposed the highest import duties on U.S. trading partners since the Great Depression, although rates have fluctuated amid legal challenges.
Botchwey said that creating stronger economies is essential given the trade wars: “It’s an opportunity we cannot miss.”

item.title: Photos show elaborate preparations for Thailand’s Royal Barges Procession
item.description:
Photos show elaborate preparations for Thailand’s Royal Barges Procession BySAKCHAI LALIT Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 8:44 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BANGKOK -- More than 2,000 oarsmen have spent months preparing for a centuries-old Thai royal tradition that will fill Bangkok’s Chao Phraya River with a fleet of intricately decorated barges on Friday.
The Royal Barge Procession is held in time for the annual Buddhist Kathin ceremony, which takes place after the end of Buddhist Lent. Buddhists offer kathin robes to monks who have remained in their monasteries throughout the three-month retreat in the rainy season.
The fleet, consisting of a total of 52 barges, will take King Maha Vajiralongkorn, Queen Suthida and members of the royal family to the Wat Arun Ratchawararam temple.
The 2,200 oarsmen from the Royal Thai Navy started their training in June, learning how to row the barges in unison at a navy dockyard before rehearsing in the river in late July.
The full dress rehearsals were performed twice in late October, drawing spectators along both sides of the river.
The rowers must master not only the precise movements required to maintain the fleet formation of five columns and three lines, but also the traditional boat songs performed during the procession. The songs help coordinate the rowing while portraying Thailand’s cultural tradition.
Thailand's Fine Arts Department has been restoring the wooden barges while preserving their traditional artistic details. The vessels have also undergone safety inspections and decorative work in preparation for the event.

item.title: South Africans to vote in key local elections seen as a tough test for ruling ANC
item.description:
South Africans to vote in key local elections seen as a tough test for ruling ANC
South Africans head to the polls for local government elections that will determine control of major cities and test the electoral strength of the African National Congress (ANC)ByMOGOMOTSI MAGOME Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 8:03 PM
JOHANNESBURG -- South Africans are preparing to vote in local government elections that will determine control of the country’s largest cities and test whether the African National Congress continues its electoral decline.
Voters on Wednesday will elect councilors, who will then choose mayors to oversee municipal services, including water, sanitation and rubbish collection.
But politicians campaigning this year have also faced questions about national issues, including illegal immigration, high unemployment and crime.
“I think for most voters, they assess the situation of where they are, that’s their immediate reaction. But for a party, the image that you have at national level might make your candidate at local level be overlooked,” said Sandile Mnguni, a political analyst at the University of KwaZulu-Natal.
The ANC lost its parliamentary majority in 2024 and formed a unity government with the Democratic Alliance (DA), the second-largest party, and smaller parties.
In the last municipal elections in 2021, the ANC lost control of several major cities. It governs others through coalitions.
Home to nearly 5 million people and most of South Africa’s corporate headquarters, Johannesburg is a key economic hub and a major prize for competing parties.
The city, which is currently governed by a fragile ANC-led coalition, has had nine mayors in 10 years. Political instability has been widely blamed for deteriorating infrastructure, financial mismanagement and the broader decline of the “city of gold.”

item.title: United Arab Emirates says military solutions offer no quick off-ramps to crisis with Iran
item.description:
United Arab Emirates says military solutions offer no quick off-ramps to crisis with Iran
The United Arab Emirates hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations to prevent a new confrontation between the U.S. and IranBySARAH EL DEEB Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 1:43 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
MANAMA, Bahrain -- The United Arab Emirates’ presidential adviser said Sunday that his country hopes a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations is possible to avert a new round of confrontation between the U.S. and Iran.
The Iran war, which began on Feb. 28 with joint strikes by the U.S. and Israel followed by attacks by Iran on the Gulf nations, has made it “a watershed year” for the region and the world, UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said at a security forum in Bahrain.
“We don’t really want to see another round of confrontation in the region,” Gargash told the audience at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security summit in Bahrain organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, or IISS, that brings together regional and international state, defense and foreign-affairs officials and experts.
Iranian negotiators are in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz soon, according to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. He said that no direct talks are being held with the U.S. and that the final outcome depends on answers provided by the United States to the “Iranian questions.”
In an interview shared on his Telegram channel, Araghchi said Iran hoped that the U.S. would choose “diplomacy over other paths.” He said Iran was ready for both defense and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality.”
A possible escalation cast a long shadow over the three-day security forum in Bahrain's capital, Manama.

item.title: UN’s peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years following US-Russia standoff
item.description:
UN’s peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years following US-Russia standoff
The U.N.'s peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has ended after 35 years due to a U.S.-Russia standoffByAKRAM OUBACHIR Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 1:34 PM
Share
CASABLANCA, Morocco -- The U.N.'s long-running peacekeeping mission for the disputed Western Sahara ceased operations Sunday after 35 years, as a result of a U.S.-Russia standoff at U.N. headquarters over the territory’s future.
The end of the mission raises concerns about stability in the region. Rich in minerals and fisheries, Western Sahara is a vast desert territory roughly the size of Colorado along Africa’s northwestern Atlantic coast. Once ruled by Spain, it is claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front.
“This 1 November 2026 marks the start of the liquidation period,” Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the U.N. secretary general, said in a statement. “A smaller team reporting to the United Nations’ Department of Operational Support will oversee the orderly transportation of assets belonging to troop-contributing countries to their respective nations, and the appropriate disposal of equipment belonging to the United Nations.''
The mission had been repeatedly extended since it was established in 1991. In the U.N. Security Council on Friday, Russia vetoed a draft U.S. resolution that would have supported Morocco’s demand for sovereignty over Western Sahara and ended the peacekeeping mission next year.
Then a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission was voted down. The disagreement led to an abrupt end of the force’s mandate.
Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the non-renewal of the mission. It called it an “instrument to internationalize the dispute.''

item.title: Thousands of volunteers build 108 stupas in a day in Bhutan's Gelephu Mindfulness City
item.description:
Thousands of volunteers build 108 stupas in a day in Bhutan's Gelephu Mindfulness City
Buddhist masters have gathered in Gelephu, Bhutan, to witness the construction of 108 stupas in a single dayByANUPAM NATH Associated Press and DEEPA BHARATH Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 1:27 PM
Share
GELEPHU, Bhutan -- Buddhist masters from various schools and denominations and about 200,000 people from around the world congregated in Gelephu, Bhutan, on Sunday to witness volunteers erect 108 stupas in a single day.
The newly erected sacred structures, representing Buddha’s enlightenment, anchor Gelephu Mindfulness City. Conceived by Bhutan’s King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck and designed by Danish architects, the city is taking shape as a vibrant economic hub that puts the ideals of ecological sustainability and the happiness of the country's citizens over commercial profit.
The city, currently a small town with a population of about 10,000, is in southern Bhutan along the border with India, about 150 miles (240 kilometers) south of Thimphu, the nation's capital.
Amid massive economic challenges — from rising unemployment and falling birth rates to the mass migration of skilled workers — Bhutanese are pinning their hopes on this city to boost their economy and provide the opportunities that would encourage young people to stay in the country.
Bhutan’s Project 108 is an initiative to install 108 stupas with each standing about 50 feet (15 meters) tall, spaced about 354 feet (108 meters) apart, in a single file along the Mao Chhu river, to appear like a “procession” of monuments, according to the project's website. The number 108 is sacred in Buddhism, which is widely practiced in Bhutan.
These stupas are known as Jangchub Chortens in Vajrayana Buddhism, a major branch that emerged in India around the 5th and 7th centuries B.C. It aims to help practitioners attain enlightenment within a single lifetime.

item.title: Canada's Carney reports progress in trade talks with US. Trump talks up 'concept' of a deal
item.description:
Canada's Carney reports progress in trade talks with US. Trump talks up 'concept' of a deal
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he had a constructive conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump about a potential trade dealByROB GILLIES Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 12:00 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
TORONTO -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday he had a constructive conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump about a potential trade deal, with negotiators set to work toward an agreement in the coming weeks as the countries seek to resolve their bitter trade dispute just days before the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump subsequently said both sides had “the concept" of a mutually beneficial deal.
Carney said the conversation built on recent discussions about the outlines of a deal that would create jobs, lower costs for families and protect Canada’s languages, culture and sovereignty.
“Our teams will now be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome,” Carney wrote on social media.
Hours later, after landing in Iowa for a rally, Trump said, “We have the concept of a very good deal with Canada.”
“We’ve been losing money for many years with Canada, many many years,” he said. “So we have — we are now very close to having a deal.”
The U.S. president mentioned speaking with Carney on Saturday and said the possible agreement is “going to be great for our farmers, great for our country, and it’ll be fine for Canada.”
Trump said the negotiations involved construction of the Keystone XL pipeline and prospects that the agreement could erase tariffs paid by U.S. farmers for Canadian products.
“Part of the agreement is that our farmers will have to pay no tariffs,” he said, even though his comments also made clear that final details had not yet been established.
